---
title: "A one-GPU setup for interpretability experiments"
description: "Caching activations without filling the disk, and the hook pattern I reuse everywhere."
date: 2026-08-02
categories: [tooling, workflow]
---

Most of what I run fits on a single GPU if the activations never all exist at
once. The pattern below is what I keep coming back to.

## Hook once, write straight to disk

```{python}
#| eval: false
from contextlib import contextmanager
import torch

@contextmanager
def capture(module, store, key):
    """Append this module's output to `store[key]`, on CPU, then detach."""
    def hook(_m, _inp, out):
        store.setdefault(key, []).append(out.detach().to("cpu", torch.float16))
    handle = module.register_forward_hook(hook)
    try:
        yield store
    finally:
        handle.remove()
```

Two details do most of the work: `float16` on the way out halves the disk cost
with no visible effect on anything I've measured, and `.to("cpu")` inside the
hook keeps the GPU from accumulating a batch's worth of residual stream.

## Three habits worth the friction

- **One run, one directory, one config file.** If you can't reconstruct which
  checkpoint produced a figure, the figure isn't evidence.
- **Save the tokenizer output, not just the text.** Re-tokenizing later with a
  slightly different version is a silent source of mismatch.
- **Write the negative results down the same day.** They are the ones you will
  otherwise re-run in four months.
